newsitem.title: USA: Republican, Clinton upbeat on budget, tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Republican, Clinton upbeat on budget, tax deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders said on Sunday they were close to clinching a deal on legislation to cut taxes and balance the budget over five years.
After a day of internal meetings and phone calls with administration officials, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said "virtually nothing" was left to resolve.

In Los Angeles, Clinton described the emerging deal to balance the budget by 2000 and cut taxes by $85 billion as a "great opportunity" and said it could be completed as early as Monday if "remaining problems" were resolved.
Congressional aides said both sides had made concessions on contentious tax issues that had held up an agreement. Lawmakers said they expected a budget deal by Monday night.
But some White House officials were more cautious.

"There are still important issues such as who gets the tax cut and children's health care that are unresolved and critical to a sound balanced budget agreement," Gene Sperling, White House economic adviser, said in a telephone interview.
"Nothing is agreed to on the tax package until everything is agreed to," he said.
Spokesman Joe Lockhart, with Clinton in Los Angeles, also tried to soften the president's remarks, saying there was no guarantee that "tomorrow is the day."
Some key details of the budget deal were emerging on Capitol Hill.

Republicans were expected to drop a provision that would not tax investment profits attributable to inflation. Clinton has strongly opposed that capital gains "indexing" plan, contending it could worsen the budget deficit in later years.
An expected White House compromise on the capital gains tax would allow cutting the top rate to 20 percent from 28 percent, congressional sources said.
The White House was expected to go along with Republican demands to let upper-middle income taxpayers claim a $500 per child tax credit by placing the income ceiling at $110,000.

Republicans showed willingness to expand the child credit to more low-income workers, which the White House has sought. But they want the administration to agree to reform a tax subsidy for the working poor, the Earned Income Tax Credit.

Proposals to make affluent seniors pay higher Medicare premiums, gradually raise the programme eligibility age to 67 from 65 and institute a $5 co-payment for home health visits would not be included in the final deal, aides said.
The legislation will call for a commission to suggest long-term Medicare reforms.

The White House showed a willingness for a higher education tax package amounting closer to $30 billion over five years than the $35 billion Clinton has insisted on. But the package was expected to include the president's programme for a $1,500 HOPE scholarship tax credit for higher education costs and a 20 percent tuition tax deduction.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said the final tax bill would make progress on his priority issue of expanding Individual Retirement Accounts.

The legislation was also expected to include a tobacco tax increase. The Senate bill would raise $15 billion over five years from a 20-cents-per-pack cigarette tax increase. But congressional aides said a tobacco tax increase would be less than that, and Republicans in meetings had discussed an increase in the 15-17-cents per pack range. Some of the revenues were likely to be directed to children's health.
The two sides were still discussing details of the children's health plan. They were planning a programme that would let governors run their own programmes, choosing from a menu of insurance options.
There were disagreements about the scope of the insurance coverage and an effort to narrow the amount of money that could be used for services, like vaccinations, rather than insurance policies.
